various applications or their recent development. Each method is elucidated through a simple

blocks.content: Figure 8.1, the AHP decision hierarchy in the general case. A green rounded box at the top reads "Goal: Rank m alternatives considering n criteria". Below it a row of five blue boxes — Criterion 1, Criterion 2, Criterion 3, an ellipsis box, and Criterion n — each joined to the goal. Below those a row of four peach boxes — Alternative 1, Alternative 2, an ellipsis box, and Alternative m. Every criterion is joined to every alternative, which is the property that makes the hierarchy complete: AHP asks for a pairwise comparison of the alternatives under each criterion in turn. The edges are plain lines with no arrowheads, so the diagram asserts membership rather than direction — contrast Figure 8.3, where the ANP version is drawn with arrows.

The AHP method, originally developed by Saaty (1977, 1990), is based on decision-makers’ 
subjective pairwise comparisons. To facilitate this, Saaty’s fundamental 1–9 scale (Table 8.4) 
is typically employed. The AHP method begins by constructing a decision hierarchy, 
organizing the overall goal, 𝑛 criteria, and 𝑚 alternatives into a structured model, as illustrated 
in Figure 8.1. Decision-makers then perform subjective pairwise comparisons to assess the 
relative importance among each pair of criteria using Saaty’s 1–9 scale. These comparisons 
are c

Analytic Network Process (ANP) 
The ANP method, developed by Saaty (1996, 1999), is a generalization and an advanced 
version of the AHP method described in Section 8.4. This more advanced meth

summary.text: Concludes the limitations of AHP (rank reversal and exponential growth in pairwise comparisons) and opens Section 8.5 on the Analytic Network Process (ANP, Saaty 1996, 1999), contrasting ANP's generalized network of clusters, inner/outer dependencies, and feedback loops with AHP's strict hierarchy and setting up a simplified 2-alternative (A1, A2), 3-criterion (C1: Cost, C2: Technical Feasibility, C3: Market Risk) example in Step 1.

blocks.content: Figure 8.3, the ANP representation of a simplified version of the same problem — the figure that shows what ANP adds to AHP. The green goal box ("Goal: Rank m alternatives considering n criteria") feeds three blue criteria boxes, and two peach alternative boxes sit below. Two things differ from Figure 8.1. Every edge now carries an arrowhead, so direction is asserted; and the criteria are joined to one another by dash-dot double-headed arrows — Criterion 1 to Criterion 2, Criterion 2 to Criterion 3, and Criterion 1 to Criterion 3 in an arc over the top — which is the interdependence AHP's hierarchy forbids. The alternatives also point back up into the criteria as well as receiving arrows from them, so the feedback runs both ways.

Unlike the AHP matrix in Figure 8.2(b), the criteria-to-criteria block is not zero (C1 column: C2 0.083333, C3 0.166667; C2 column: C1 0.125000, C3 0.125000; C3 column: C1 0.187500, C2 0.062500) and the alternatives feed back into the criteria (A1 column: C2 0.333333, C3 0.666667; A2 column: C2 0.500000, C3 0.500000). That non-zero feedback is the structural difference the chapter is illustrating.

Figure 8.4(b), the limit supermatrix W∞ for the same ANP model, in the same SuperDecisions window. The structural fact to read off it: **every column is identical**, each holding C1 0.079748, C2 0.199064, C3 0.292616, A1 0.240932, A2 0.187639, with Goal_Node 0.000000. That is what convergence of a column-stochastic supermatrix to its limit means — the long-run priority no longer depends on where the walk started — and it is why ANP reads its answer off any single column. A "Done" button is at the foot of the window.
